title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 2
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Practice test
summary: A full end-of-Stage-8 maths test in Checkpoint style: two 1-hour papers of 50 marks (Paper 1 no calculator, Paper 2 calculator) set around a family holiday in Alexandria, a garden design, a school canteen survey, taxi fares, a cycling race and tiling patterns — with full worked solutions and a mark scheme.

items: This is an **end-of-Stage-8 practice test** in the style of Cambridge Lower Secondary maths tests. The Cambridge Checkpoint test itself is taken at the end of Stage 9; this test checks the Stage 8 work that Checkpoint builds on.
It has **two papers**, like the Stage 8 Progression Test: **Paper 1** — 1 hour, 50 marks, **no calculator**. **Paper 2** — 1 hour, 50 marks, **calculator allowed**.
Equipment: a pen, a pencil, a ruler, a protractor and compasses (geometrical instruments). Tracing paper is optional. Use a calculator in Paper 2 only.

Answer **all** the questions. The marks for each part are shown with the question. For questions worth 2 or 3 marks, show your working — you can get a mark for a correct method even if the final answer is wrong.
Do one paper at a time with the timer on, in a quiet place. **Write on paper first if you like** — you can print the question paper (PDF) below and type your answers in at the end.

**How marking works here:** typed answers (numbers, short answers and multiple choice) are checked automatically. Written answers (explanations, constructions and working) you mark yourself with the mark scheme shown after you finish — be strict, as a real examiner would be.
Your score is a **practice score** to show you what to revise. It is not an official Cambridge result.

blocks.title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 2
blocks.intro: Two papers, 1 hour each, 50 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed. Answer all questions and show your working on paper. Type fractions like 3/4, mixed numbers like 2 1/4, powers like x^2 and coordinates like (2, −1). Where a question asks you to explain, construct or show working, mark yourself with the mark scheme at the end.

questions.p: Question 1
questions.e: Indices first: 3^{2} = 9. Then × and ÷ from left to right: 4 × 9 = 36, 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Subtract last: 20 − 6 = **14**. (Working left to right gives 16 × 9 ÷ 6 = 24, which is wrong.)

questions.p: Question 1
questions.q: (b) Brackets are added to 5 + 3 × 4 − 2 so that the answer is 30. Which one is correct?

questions.p: Question 2
Question 2
questions.q:
(b) Ali says: “When you multiply three negative integers together, the answer is always negative.”
Is Ali correct? Explain how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Yes (correct) with a correct reason, e.g. negative × negative = positive, then positive × negative = negative; or a general argument using signs. Accept a correct example with the sign rule stated, e.g. (−2) × (−3) × (−4) = 6 × (−4) = −24. Do not accept a single example with no reason (one example does not show it is ALWAYS true). Do not accept ‘No’.
questions.e: Yes. Multiply the first two: negative × negative = positive. Then positive × the third negative = negative. This works for any three negative integers, e.g. (−2) × (−3) × (−4) = 6 × (−4) = −24.

questions.p:
Question 3
The Hassan family drive from Cairo to Alexandria for their summer holiday. The road distance is about 200 km.
questions.q: Use 1 km ≈ 5/8 of a mile to find the distance in miles.

questions.p:
Question 4
On holiday the Hassan family drink 2 3/4 litres of bottled water each day.
questions.q: (a) How many litres do they drink in 6 days? Give your answer as a mixed number.
questions.e:
Estimate first: 6 × 3 = 18, so the answer is a bit less than 18. 6 × 2 3/4 = 6 × 2 + 6 × 3/4 = 12 + 18/4 = 12 + 4 1/2 = **16 1/2 litres**.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 16 1/2 (oe, e.g. 33/2 or 16.5). 1 mark for 12 + 18/4 or 6 × 11/4 = 66/4 seen.

questions.p:
Question 4
On holiday the Hassan family drink 2 3/4 litres of bottled water each day.
questions.q: (b) They pour a 9-litre bottle of water into cups. Each cup holds 3/4 of a litre. How many cups can they fill?
questions.e: 9 ÷ 3/4 = 9 × 4/3 = 36/3 = **12 cups**. (There are 4 quarters in each litre, so 36 quarters, and 36 ÷ 3 = 12.)

questions.p:
Question 4

questions.q: (c) On Monday the family walk 4 1/3 km along the Corniche. On Tuesday they walk 1 3/4 km. How much further do they walk on Monday? Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.
questions.e:
Estimate: 4 − 2 = 2, so about 2 or 3 km. 4 1/3 − 1 3/4 = 13/3 − 7/4 = 52/12 − 21/12 = 31/12 = **2 7/12 km**. (Or: 4 1/3 − 1 = 3 1/3, then 3 4/12 − 9/12 = 2 16/12 − 9/12 = 2 7/12.)
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 2 7/12 cao. 1 mark for a correct common denominator seen, e.g. 52/12 − 21/12 or 4/12 and 9/12, or for 31/12 not written as a mixed number.

questions.p:
Question 5
A hotel room in Alexandria cost E£800 a night last summer. This summer the same room costs E£920 a night.
questions.q: (a) Work out the absolute change in the price.
questions.e: Absolute change = new − old = 920 − 800 = **E£120** (an increase).

questions.p:
Question 5
A hotel room in Alexandria cost E£800 a night last summer. This summer the same room costs E£920 a night.
questions.q: (b) Work out the percentage increase in the price.
questions.e:
Percentage increase = change ÷ original × 100 = 120 ÷ 800 × 100. 120/800 = 12/80 = 3/20 = 15/100, so **15%**.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 15. 1 mark for 120/800 (oe) seen. Do not divide by the new price: 120 ÷ 920 is wrong.

questions.p: Question 6
questions.e: Multiply → add the indices; divide → subtract: 7 + 2 − 4 = 5, so **n = 5**.

questions.p: Question 6
questions.q: (b) Write down the value of ∛(−64).
questions.e: (−4) × (−4) × (−4) = 16 × (−4) = −64, so ∛(−64) = **−4**. A negative number has a negative cube root.

questions.p: Question 6
questions.e: (−5)^{2} = 25 (negative squared is positive). (−2)^{3} = −8 (negative cubed is negative). 25 − (−8) = 25 + 8 = **33**.

questions.p: Question 7
questions.q: Work out 0.72 ÷ 0.01
questions.e: Dividing by 0.01 is the same as multiplying by 100: 0.72 × 100 = **72**.

questions.p: Question 8
questions.q: (a) Which fraction is equal to a recurring decimal?
questions.e: 3/8 = 0.375, 7/20 = 0.35 and 9/25 = 0.36 all stop (terminate). **5/12** = 0.41666…, the 6 recurs. A fraction in its simplest form terminates only when the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5; 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 has a factor 3.

questions.p: Question 8
questions.q:
(b) Zara says: “7/30 is a terminating decimal, because 30 is a multiple of 10.”
Is Zara correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No, with a correct reason, e.g. 7/30 = 0.2333… (the 3 recurs); or 30 = 2 × 3 × 5 has a prime factor 3 (7/30 is already in simplest form); or 7/30 = 0.7 ÷ 3 = 0.2333… Do not accept ‘No’ with no reason or a wrong reason.
questions.e: Zara is **not correct**. 7/30 = 0.7 ÷ 3 = 0.2333…, so it recurs. 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, and the factor 3 makes the decimal recur. Being a multiple of 10 is not enough.

questions.p: Question 8
questions.q: (c) Which list is in order, starting with the smallest?
questions.e: Write as decimals: −2/3 = −0.666…, −0.65, −5/8 = −0.625, −0.6. For negative numbers the one furthest from zero is the smallest: **−2/3 < −0.65 < −5/8 < −0.6**. The first list is the right order but largest first.

questions.p: Question 9
questions.q: Work out 8.64 ÷ 0.4
questions.e:
Multiply both numbers by 10 so you divide by a whole number: 86.4 ÷ 4 = **21.6**. Estimate: 8 ÷ 0.4 = 20 ✓.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 21.6. 1 mark for 86.4 ÷ 4 seen, or for an answer with the correct digits 216 (e.g. 2.16 or 216).

questions.p: Question 10
questions.q: Show how to work out 3.7 × 46 + 3.7 × 54 without a calculator. Write down the answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 370 with a method using the distributive law, e.g. 3.7 × (46 + 54) = 3.7 × 100 = 370. Accept 370 from correct long multiplications (170.2 + 199.8 = 370).

questions.p: Question 11
questions.q: (a) Which one of these is a formula?
c: P = 4s, where P is the perimeter of a square of side s
questions.e: **P = 4s** is a formula: it connects two quantities and works for every value of s. 4x + 3 is an expression (no = sign). 4x + 3 = 19 is an equation (true for one value, x = 4). x > 4 is an inequality.

questions.p: Question 11
questions.q: (b) Simplify 3a^{2} + 5a − a^{2} + 2a
questions.e: Collect like terms: 3a^{2} − a^{2} = 2a^{2}; 5a + 2a = 7a. Answer **2a^{2} + 7a**. a^{2} and a are not like terms, so they cannot be added. Type a^{2} as a^2.

questions.p: Question 11
questions.q: (c) Expand 2x(x^{2} − 3)

questions.p: Question 11
questions.q: (d) Factorise completely 12y^{2} + 18y
questions.e:
The HCF of 12y^{2} and 18y is 6y. 12y^{2} ÷ 6y = 2y and 18y ÷ 6y = 3, so **6y(2y + 3)**. Check by expanding: 12y^{2} + 18y ✓.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 6y(2y + 3). 1 mark for a correct partial factorisation, e.g. 6(2y^{2} + 3y), 3y(4y + 6) or 2y(6y + 9).

questions.p: Question 12
questions.q: (a) Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 11
questions.e: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 7 = 11. Add 7: 3x = 18. Divide by 3: **x = 6**. Check: 5 × 6 − 7 = 23 and 2 × 6 + 11 = 23 ✓.
questions.ms: Answer x = 6. 2 marks for x = 6 with working. 1 mark for a correct first step, e.g. 3x − 7 = 11, 5x = 2x + 18 or 3x = 18. Accept x = 6 from trial and improvement only if a check is shown (2 marks). Do not award marks for 6 with wrong working (nfww).

questions.p: Question 12
questions.q: (b) Solve (x + 4)/3 = 5
questions.e: Multiply both sides by 3: x + 4 = 15. Subtract 4: **x = 11**.

Which inequality is shown?
questions.e: The open (empty) circle at −2 means −2 is **not** included, so −2 < x. The filled circle at 3 means 3 **is** included, so x ≤ 3. Answer: **−2 < x ≤ 3**.

questions.e:
The sequence goes up by 2 each time, so it starts 2n. When n = 1, 2n = 2, but there are 8 tiles, so add 6: **2n + 6**. Check n = 3: 2 × 3 + 6 = 12 ✓. (Picture reason: 3 rows of n + 2 tiles is 3n + 6 tiles, minus the n blue tiles = 2n + 6.)
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 2n + 6 (oe). 1 mark for 2n + c where c ≠ 6, or for 2n seen.

questions.ms: 1 mark for a correct reason, e.g. 2n + 6 is always even and 75 is odd; or 2n + 6 = 75 gives n = 34.5, which is not a whole number; or the pattern numbers next to 75 have 74 (n = 34) and 76 (n = 35) white tiles. Do not accept ‘75 is too big’.
questions.e: The number of white tiles 2n + 6 = 2(n + 3) is always **even**, but 75 is odd. (Or: 2n + 6 = 75 gives 2n = 69, n = 34.5, which is not a pattern number.)

questions.p: Question 14
questions.q:
(a) Here is a function machine:
input → × 3 → − 4 → output
The output is 17. Work out the input.
questions.e: Work backwards with inverse operations: 17 + 4 = 21, then 21 ÷ 3 = **7**. Check: 7 × 3 − 4 = 17 ✓.

questions.p: Question 14
questions.q: (b) Which line is parallel to y = 3x − 2?
questions.e: Parallel lines have the same gradient m. y = 3x − 2 has gradient 3, and so does **y = 3x + 5**. y = −3x − 2 has the same y-intercept (−2), not the same gradient.

questions.p:
Question 15
Omar is drawing a tiling pattern. He says: “A rhombus is a special kind of square.”
questions.q: Explain why Omar is wrong.
questions.ms: 1 mark for a correct explanation, e.g. a rhombus does not need right angles (a square must have four right angles); OR it is the other way round: every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square. Accept a sketch of a rhombus without right angles with a correct comment.
questions.e: A square has 4 equal sides **and** 4 right angles. A rhombus only needs 4 equal sides; its angles do not have to be 90°. So every square is a special rhombus, but a rhombus is not always a square. Omar has it the wrong way round.

Question 18
Use a ruler and compasses only. Do not rub out your construction arcs.
questions.q: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.
questions.ms: 2 marks: an accurate triangle (all three sides correct to within 2 mm) with both pairs of construction arcs seen. 1 mark: an accurate triangle without arcs, OR correct arcs (radius 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B, or the other way round) with one side wrong by more than 2 mm.
questions.e: 1) Draw AB = 7 cm with a ruler. 2) Open the compasses to 5 cm, put the point on A and draw an arc above AB. 3) Open the compasses to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc. 4) Where the arcs cross is C. Join AC and BC. Check with a ruler: AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm. Leave the arcs — they show your method.

questions.p: Question 19
questions.q:
(a) A boat sails from the harbour in Alexandria on a bearing of 065° to a fishing area.
Work out the bearing of the harbour from the fishing area.
questions.e: The back bearing is 180° more (because 065° is less than 180°): 65 + 180 = **245°**.

questions.p: Question 19
questions.q:
(b) On a plan of a garden, a straight path goes from P(−3, 4) to Q(5, −2). A bench is at the midpoint of PQ.
Work out the coordinates of the bench.
questions.e: Midpoint = (mean of the x-coordinates, mean of the y-coordinates) = ((−3 + 5)/2, (4 + (−2))/2) = (2/2, 2/2) = **(1, 1)**.

The school canteen sells a meal deal. Students choose one main and one drink.
Mains: rice, pasta, sandwich
Drinks: water, juice, milk, lemonade
questions.q: (a) List all the possible meal deals, or show them in a table.
questions.ms: 1 mark for all 12 combinations listed or shown in a correct table (3 × 4), with no repeats. Abbreviations (e.g. R/W, P/J) are fine.
questions.e: Use a table: rows rice, pasta, sandwich; columns water, juice, milk, lemonade. 3 × 4 = **12** meal deals: RW, RJ, RM, RL, PW, PJ, PM, PL, SW, SJ, SM, SL.

questions.p:
Question 20
The school canteen sells a meal deal. Students choose one main and one drink.
Mains: rice, pasta, sandwich
Drinks: water, juice, milk, lemonade
questions.q: (b) Laila chooses a main and a drink at random. Find the probability that she chooses pasta and juice.
questions.e: There are 12 equally likely meal deals and only 1 is pasta with juice, so P = **1/12**.

questions.p:
Question 20
The school canteen sells a meal deal. Students choose one main and one drink.
Mains: rice, pasta, sandwich
Drinks: water, juice, milk, lemonade
questions.q:
(c) The probability that the canteen sells out of sandwiches on a school day is 0.15.
Find the probability that the canteen does not sell out of sandwiches on a school day.
questions.e: ‘Sells out’ and ‘does not sell out’ are complementary events, so their probabilities add to 1: 1 − 0.15 = **0.85**.

Total in Egyptian pounds: 5 × 450 = E£2250. Change to pounds: 2250 ÷ 61.40 = 36.6449… = **£36.64** to the nearest penny.

Question 2
The price of a train ticket from Cairo to Alexandria goes up from E£85 to E£102.
questions.q: Work out the percentage increase.
questions.e:
Increase = 102 − 85 = 17. Percentage increase = 17 ÷ 85 × 100 = **20%**. (Or multiplier: 102 ÷ 85 = 1.2, which is a 20% increase.)
Mark scheme: 2 marks for 20. 1 mark for 17 ÷ 85 or 102 ÷ 85 = 1.2 seen.

questions.q: (b) One stage of the race is 5 km long. How many complete turns does the wheel make in this stage?
questions.e: 5 km = 5 × 1000 × 100 = 500 000 cm. 500 000 ÷ 213.628… = 2340.5… So the wheel makes **2340 complete turns** (round down: the 2341st turn is not finished).
questions.ms: Answer 2340. 2 marks for 2340. 1 mark for 500 000 ÷ their circumference seen (e.g. 500 000 ÷ 213.6), OR for 2340.5… or 2341 as the answer. The units must match: using 5000 (metres) with the circumference in cm scores 0.

(g) A garden lamp is a 3D shape with 12 vertices and 18 edges.
Use Euler's formula to work out the number of faces.
questions.e: Euler's formula: V − E + F = 2 (or F + V − E = 2). 12 − 18 + F = 2, so F = **8**. (This could be a hexagonal prism: 2 hexagons + 6 rectangles.)

A tile designer works with square tiles. A rectangular wall panel is 84 cm by 120 cm. It is covered exactly with identical square tiles, with no cutting. The tiles are as large as possible.
questions.q: (a) What is the side length of each tile?
questions.e: The side must divide both 84 and 120, and be as large as possible: the HCF. 84 = 2^{2} × 3 × 7 and 120 = 2^{3} × 3 × 5, so HCF = 2^{2} × 3 = **12 cm**.

Which question gives continuous data?

questions.ms: 1 mark for a sensible reason, e.g. only students who use the canteen are asked (students with packed lunches are left out); students at the front may be from one class or year group; it is only one day; 30 is a small sample; students in the queue probably like the canteen. questions.e: It is a biased sample: everyone asked is already queuing, so students who bring a packed lunch (and may dislike the canteen) are not asked. Also the first 30 may all be from the same class or year, and it is only one day.

Question 10
Laila makes a spinner with 4 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. She spins it 200 times. It lands on 4 a total of 62 times.
questions.q: (a) Write down the experimental probability of the spinner landing on 4.
questions.e: Experimental probability = number of times ÷ number of trials = 62/200 = **0.31** (31/100).

questions.p:
Question 10
Laila makes a spinner with 4 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. She spins it 200 times. It lands on 4 a total of 62 times.
questions.q: (b) If the spinner is fair, how many times would you expect it to land on 4 in 200 spins?
questions.e: Theoretical probability = 1/4. Expected number = 1/4 × 200 = **50**.

questions.p:
Question 10
Laila makes a spinner with 4 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. She spins it 200 times. It lands on 4 a total of 62 times.
questions.q: (c) Laila wants a more reliable estimate of the probability of landing on 4. What should she do?
questions.ms: 1 mark for: spin it many more times (e.g. 1000 or more trials), or repeat the experiment and combine the results. Do not accept ‘spin it again’ without saying more times, or ‘make it fair’.
questions.e: Do **many more spins** (for example 1000). The more trials, the closer the experimental probability usually gets to the true probability. Then compare it with the theoretical 0.25.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the worked solution for **every** question, including the ones you got right — check that your method was efficient and your working was clear.

Make a list of the questions you lost marks on and write down why: a wrong method, a careless slip, a missing unit, or not reading the question (e.g. ‘simplest form’, ‘complete turns’, ‘1 decimal place’).

Fractions, decimals, percentages and ratio (Paper 1 Q4–Q10, Paper 2 Q1–Q2): revise **Fractions: Recurring Decimals, Mixed Numbers and Order of Operations**, **Ordering and Calculating with Decimals**, **Percentage Increase, Decrease and Absolute Change** and **Multiplying and Dividing by 0.1 and 0.01, and Significant Figures**.

Integers, powers and roots (P1 Q1, Q2, Q6; P2 Q4c, Q7a–b): revise **Order of Operations and Calculating with Integers**, **Types of Number and Index Laws**, **Squares, Cubes and Roots (Positive and Negative)** and **Factors, Multiples, Primes, HCF and LCM**.

Algebra (P1 Q11–Q14; P2 Q3, Q6f, Q7d): revise **Algebraic Expressions: Simplifying, Expanding and Factorising**, **Writing Expressions and Formulae, and Changing the Subject**, **Equations and Inequalities**, **Sequences and the nth Term**, **Functions and Straight-line Graphs (y = mx + c)** and **Reading and Interpreting Real-life Graphs**.

Geometry (P1 Q3, Q15–Q19; P2 Q4a–b, Q6, Q7c, Q8): revise **Area of Parallelograms and Trapezia**, **Volume of Prisms and Surface Area**, **Circumference of a Circle, and Miles and Kilometres**, **Angles in Triangles and on Parallel Lines**, **Constructions with Ruler and Compasses**, **Quadrilaterals and Regular Polygons**, **3D Shapes: Euler's Formula and Plans and Elevations**, **Bearings and Midpoints** and **Translation, Reflection, Rotation and Enlargement**.

Statistics and probability (P1 Q20; P2 Q5, Q9, Q10): revise **Data Collection and Sampling**, **Representing Data**, **Averages, Range and Comparing Distributions** and **Probability: Complementary and Combined Events**.
